mcqs.question: You open 10 tabs in Chrome. Roughly how many OS processes should you expect, and why not exactly 10?
options: Exactly 10 — one process handles everything for each tab in isolation
1 total — Chrome multiplexes all tabs inside a single process for efficiency
Around 10 renderer processes plus a shared browser, GPU, and network process, since those last three aren't duplicated per tab
40 or more — each tab gets 4 dedicated processes with none shared
mcqs.explanation: The browser, GPU, and network processes are shared infrastructure, not per-tab — only the renderer is typically one-per-site-instance. That's why memory doesn't scale as cleanly as "10 tabs = 10x one tab."

mcqs.question: Under what circumstance might a browser NOT give two different-origin iframes on the same page fully separate renderer processes?
options: When both frames are under embedder-imposed resource limits, such as on a memory-constrained mobile device
When the two origins share the same top-level domain suffix
When both pages are served over HTTPS
Never — every distinct origin always gets a dedicated process with no exceptions
mcqs.explanation: Site isolation's default is per-origin processes, but browsers trade some of that isolation for memory savings under real resource pressure, notably on low-memory devices. Shared TLD or HTTPS-ness don't factor into the process-assignment decision at all.

mcqs.question: A hot function gets JIT-optimized by V8, then later 'deoptimizes' back to bytecode. What most commonly triggers that?
options: The GPU process signals that it needs the CPU budget back
A fixed timer expires and all optimized code is periodically discarded
The optimizer's assumption about the shape or type of an argument turned out to be wrong on a later call
The renderer process is about to be recycled by the browser process
mcqs.explanation: JIT compilers optimize aggressively based on observed call shapes; when a later call breaks that assumption (e.g. a number argument suddenly becomes a string), the optimized code is no longer valid and the engine falls back to the safe, slower bytecode path.

mcqs.question: Your app has a layout bug reported only on Firefox for Android and iOS Chrome, but not desktop Chrome. What's the most useful next step given how engines are distributed?
options: Assume it's an Android-only bug, since both reports mention mobile
Test in Gecko (Firefox's engine) and WebKit (which iOS Chrome also uses under Apple's policy) specifically, rather than more Chromium browsers
Ignore the iOS Chrome report since Chrome should behave identically everywhere
File it as a Blink bug, since Chrome is involved in one of the reports
mcqs.explanation: iOS Chrome is Chrome in name only — Apple requires it to embed WebKit, so the bug pattern points at Gecko and WebKit specifically, not at "Chrome" as a brand. More Chromium-based testing wouldn't reproduce either report.

mcqs.question: Why is 'one page equals one renderer process' not a safe assumption to make when reasoning about a page's behavior?
options: Because a single page can span multiple renderer processes when it embeds cross-origin iframes, since site isolation splits by origin
Because every page always uses exactly one process per DOM node it contains
Because renderer processes are shared across all open tabs by default in every browser
Because GPU compositing always merges every open page into a single process
mcqs.explanation: Site isolation assigns processes per origin, not per tab, so a page embedding cross-site iframes (ads, payment widgets) can genuinely be backed by several renderer processes at once — the reverse of the naive one-page-one-process picture.
